title: Two Pointers & Sliding Window
html:
Two Pointers & Sliding Window

Both replace a nested loop with a single pass by exploiting structure the nested loop ignores - usually sortedness, or the fact that a window's answer can be updated rather than recomputed.

Two pointers

Converging - one from each end, moving inward. Works when the data is sorted and the comparison at each step says which end to move. Pair-sum in a sorted array: too small and the left must rise, too large and the right must fall. Each step eliminates a whole row of the comparison matrix, which is why one pass suffices.

Same direction, fast and slow - one reads, the other writes. In-place removal and de-duplication are this: the write pointer marks where the next kept element goes, so the kept prefix is always valid.

Cycle detection - advance one by one and the other by two. If a cycle exists they meet inside it, because the gap between them changes by exactly one per step. Meeting is guaranteed, not lucky.

Sliding window

A contiguous range that grows on the right and shrinks on the left while maintaining a running answer.

The requirement is that the answer be incrementally updatable: adding one element and removing one must both be cheap. Sums, counts and frequency maps qualify. "The median of the window" does not, without a heavier structure.

Fixed size - slide by adding the entrant and removing the leaver.

Variable size - grow until a condition breaks, shrink until it holds. Longest substring without repeats, smallest window covering a target. Each index enters once and leaves once, so despite the inner shrink loop the total is O(n), not O(n squared). That is the part that looks wrong and is not.

The monotonicity trap

Variable windows depend on a condition that, once broken, stays broken until you shrink. "Sum at most k" works because adding never helps. "Sum exactly k" does not work when negatives are present: growing can bring the sum back down, so shrinking on violation discards valid answers. With negatives, prefix sums plus a map is the correct tool.

Choosing

  • Sorted input, looking for a pair or triple - converging pointers.
  • Contiguous range with a constraint - sliding window.
  • Reordering in place without extra space - fast and slow pointers.
  • Not contiguous, or a non-monotonic constraint - neither.

Common mistakes

  • Never shrinking, and reporting the whole array.
  • Updating the answer before restoring the invariant rather than after.
  • Off by one in the length: right - left + 1.
  • Two pointers on unsorted data, where the direction decision means nothing.
